Photograph: Piero Cruciatti/AFP/Getty Images Protest ‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify Hundreds at Lisbon tent camp demand action, as Giorgia Meloni says march in Italy was exploited by ‘hooligans’ Sam Jones in Madrid and agencies Sun 18 Oct 2026 07.02 EDT Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 11.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal , with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up in Lisbon over the weekend. A march in central Milan on Saturday to protest against rising living costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables. Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds, and images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car. At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported. View image in fullscreen Riot police and protesters clashing in Milan. Photograph: Stringer/Anadolu/Getty Images Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that while demonstrating was a right, “setting our cities ablaze is not”. In a social media post, she said “hooligans” had exploited the protests “to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and to hold entire cities hostage”. Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said that while “the reasons for the protests were understandable, the violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable”. In Lisbon, a tent camp reminiscent of the one established in Madrid three weeks ago was set up by protesters demanding action to tackle the housing crisis and living costs. Map of protests across Europe Hundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio Square – located in the bustling, touristic heart of the Portuguese capital – after a march that had drawn thousands of people nationwide. The attenders vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square. “The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant. “So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating.” View image in fullscreen The tent camp in Rossio Square (Praça de Dom Pedro IV), Lisbon. Photograph: Manuel Fuentes/EPA Antonio Margado, a 52-year-old engineer, criticised the centre-right government for “a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less”. Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data. The impact is especially harsh on younger people and those in Lisbon – around a quarter of Portugal’s more than 11 million inhabitants live in the capital’s greater metropolitan area. Saturday’s camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that started in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents had already been set up. At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures against soaring housing costs. View image in fullscreen Protesters in Lisbon. Photograph: Filipe Amorim/AFP/Getty Images Portugal’s prime minister, Luís Montenegro, has said his government understood that people wanted to “express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies”. But he has warned political rivals against “importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society”, in a likely reference to violent protests in France . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion There have also been violent demonstrations in Albania this week , where demonstrators angry over university conditions and high tuition fees have demanded the resignation of the country’s prime minister, Edi Rama. On Saturday, protesters threw rocks, molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing. In a sign of the escalating violence, police fired rubber bullets on the demonstrators for the first time since the protests began. The protests continued into the night, with buildings – including a court, banks and post office – set on fire or severely damaged. View image in fullscreen A car on fire during an anti-government demonstration outside the prime minister’s office in Tirana on Saturday. Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/AP The unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to the family of the US president, Donald Trump. Growing anger over soaring rents and social inequality boiled over in Spain last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home because she was unable to pay the 230% rent increase sought by the investment firm that had bought her flat. The plight of the late María del Carmen Abascal – and the wider issue it embodied – led to street demonstrations and the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital , and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November. View image in fullscreen A banner depicting María del Carmen Abascal, reading ‘power to the people’, in Madrid on Friday. Photograph: Bernat Armangué/AP In France, fury over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities in schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris has snowballed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards. More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Norway and Finland say they are not acting on behalf of other European leaders By Hafsa Khalil Published 27 October 2026, 13:12 GMT Updated 2 hours ago The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - a rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders. The aim was looking at "future negotiations to help to end the war" in Ukraine, the offices of President Alexander Stubb and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said. Their initiative was not on behalf of "Europe as a whole". After the call, Putin said "confrontational" EU and Nato policies were prolonging the war which began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken to the two Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin. Last week, Zelensky met them as well as US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo. The Ukrainian leader said he was grateful for the "active support" of his Finnish and Norwegian counterparts. Tuesday's 90-minute phone call was held from the Finnish capital Helsinki, and showed "big differences in views", StÃ¸re said. Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the call to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said. The call was "frank and substantive", Stubb said, explaining that the war's outcome will "have a direct impact on our and the broader European security". StÃ¸re added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations." The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered. He - like Stubb and StÃ¸re - had agreed to continue their direct phone communication, the statement added. Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push Published 5 days ago StÃ¸re said all their allies had been informed of the call ahead of time. Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "very sceptical" of Tuesday's dialogue, telling Danish broadcaster DR, it had not been "co-ordinated with any of the rest of us". Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates, was "moderately optimistic". Relations between the US, Ukraine and its European allies have been souring since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia - allowing it to export oil to the US. But last week, Stubb, StÃ¸re and Zelesnky met Witkoff in the Norwegian capital, before the US special envoy travelled on to St Petersburg to meet Putin. Following the talks, Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to resume three-way negotiations that Russia had stopped for months. After speaking to the two Nordic leaders, Zelensky said part of their discussions with Putin had centred on November's trilateral talks to be held in Abu Dhabi. Zelensky said he had discussed with them "various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security". Stubb and StÃ¸re are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025. As the US administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to establish direct contacts with the Kremlin. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the European Union of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons. But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
